title: American Doctors Are Finally Getting Nutrition Training. It Still Will Not Cover Your Dadi's Kitchen.
excerpt: Seventy-three US medical schools have pledged 40 hours of nutrition education. For South Asian patients, that is still not the right 40 hours.
body:
The average American doctor gets fewer hours of nutrition training in medical school than a personal trainer needs to get certified at the gym. That is finally changing — but not fast enough for the communities that need it most.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced on Monday that 19 additional medical schools have pledged to require at least 40 hours of nutrition education for students starting in the fall of 2026. The new commitments bring the total to 73 schools, including the University of Maryland, Florida Atlantic University, and the University of Massachusetts. Eight accrediting and testing organisations have also agreed to strengthen nutrition training across residency programs.

It is a significant step. But for the roughly 5.4 million South Asians in the United States, the question is not just whether doctors will learn about nutrition. It is whether they will learn about *their* nutrition.

## The Knowledge Gap That Costs Lives

The average U.S. medical school currently devotes roughly 19 hours of its entire curriculum to nutrition — a number that has barely budged since the 1980s. Most of that training is confined to biochemistry lectures in the first two years, disconnected from the clinical realities of the patients doctors will eventually treat.

For South Asian patients, this creates a specific and measurable problem. The MASALA study, the largest longitudinal study of South Asian health in America, has documented that South Asian adults develop prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension at significantly higher rates than white, Black, Hispanic, and Chinese Americans — despite reporting healthier diets, lower alcohol use, and comparable exercise.

The paradox is not a paradox at all. It is a mismatch between the dietary frameworks doctors are taught and the metabolic realities of the populations they serve. A physician trained to counsel patients on the Mediterranean diet may have never encountered a patient whose daily staples are rice, daal, ghee, and roti. They may not know that the glycaemic index of basmati rice differs sharply from jasmine rice. They may not understand that paneer is not a simple substitute for tofu, or that the way cooking oil is heated in Indian kitchens changes its metabolic impact.

## Why Forty Hours Is Not Enough

The new 40-hour pledge is voluntary and its content is left to each school. The HHS initiative does not mandate specific curricula, culturally tailored modules, or population-specific training. Most schools will satisfy the requirement by expanding existing coursework on macronutrients, micronutrients, and chronic disease management — frameworks built around white, Western dietary norms.

Dr. Namratha Kandula, co-founder of the MASALA study and a professor at Northwestern University, has spent over a decade documenting how South Asian cardiovascular risk defies conventional screening timelines. Her team identified a critical window in the 40s — a full decade earlier than standard guidelines suggest — when South Asian adults already show elevated clinical risk.

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviors and clinical risk was surprising," Kandula has said. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental."

What is missing, in part, is a nutritional vocabulary that accounts for how South Asian diets interact with South Asian metabolisms. A 40-hour module that treats all populations as interchangeable will not close that gap.

## What the Diaspora Should Watch For

For NRIs navigating the American healthcare system, the implications are practical. If your doctor's nutrition training does not include the foods you actually eat, the dietary advice you receive is at best incomplete and at worst harmful.

Some institutions are beginning to address this. The South Asian Heart Center at El Camino Health in Mountain View, California, has pioneered culturally specific cardiac risk programs that account for South Asian dietary patterns, body composition, and metabolic profiles. Programs like these remain the exception.

The 73-school commitment is progress. It signals that the medical establishment is beginning to acknowledge a decades-long blind spot. But for the community that faces the widest gap between lifestyle and clinical outcomes, the question is whether more hours of the same curriculum will actually change anything.

The answer, for now, is probably not. But at least the conversation has started.

*Sources: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (June 2026), Reuters, MASALA Study / Journal of the American Heart Association, Northwestern University*
